The university's U.S. News & World Report ranking dropped from #42 to #58 during the test-optional period, partially because the methodology penalizes institutions that cannot report median test scores for the full incoming class.
cases.description: Test scores predict success and rankings reward them, but removing the requirement boosted diversity with minimal academic impact
cases.rationale: The NBER study implies tests are valuable predictors and should be kept. The university's own data shows minimal GPA difference without them. Diversity increased substantially during the test-optional period. But the ranking dropped 16 places. Each context supports a different conclusion and the tradeoffs between prediction, equity, and institutional reputation point in different directions.

cases.query: Is this school district's teacher retention strategy working?
contexts: The district implemented a $5,000 annual retention bonus for teachers with 5+ years of experience in January 2023. Since implementation, the resignation rate for eligible teachers dropped from 18% to 11% year-over-year.

An exit survey of the 47 teachers who still resigned despite the bonus found that 78% cited 'lack of administrative support' and 'excessive non-teaching duties' as their primary reasons for leaving, with only 6% mentioning compensation.

The district's total spending on retention bonuses was $3.2 million in the 2023-2024 school year, paid from a federal ESSER grant that expires in September 2025. The district's general fund budget has a projected deficit of $4.8 million for 2025-2026.

Neighboring districts have begun offering $7,000-$8,000 retention bonuses and signing bonuses of up to $10,000 for experienced teachers in shortage subjects (math, science, special education), funded by permanent local bond measures.
cases.description: Retention improved after the bonus but the root causes are non-financial, funding is temporary, and competitors are outbidding the district
cases.rationale: The resignation rate dropped from 18% to 11%, implying the strategy works. But exit surveys show the real issues are administrative, not financial, suggesting the bonus masks the problem. The funding expires in 2025 with no replacement budget. And neighboring districts are offering more, creating a future retention arms race. Success by one metric, failure by underlying analysis.

cases.query: What is the recommended treatment for mild depression?
contexts: A 2019 clinical practice guideline from the American Psychiatric Association states that SSRIs remain the first-line treatment for mild to moderate depression, citing response rates of 60-70% across multiple randomized trials.

A 2024 meta-analysis published in The Lancet Psychiatry, covering 47 trials and 12,000 patients, concludes that psychotherapy alone is as effective as SSRIs for mild depression, with significantly fewer side effects and lower relapse rates at 12-month follow-up.
cases.description: Newer meta-analysis challenges the established guideline on first-line treatment for mild depression.
cases.rationale: The 2019 guideline recommends SSRIs as first-line, but the 2024 meta-analysis of 47 trials argues psychotherapy alone is equally effective with fewer side effects, creating a temporal conflict between authoritative sources.

cases.query: How old is the universe?
contexts: NASA's 2020 measurement using the Planck satellite's cosmic microwave background data places the age of the universe at 13.77 billion years, with a margin of error of just 40 million years.

A 2023 study led by Dr. Rajendra Gupta at the University of Ottawa, published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, proposes that the universe may be 26.7 billion years old, nearly double the accepted estimate, based on a model incorporating tired light theory and evolving coupling constants.
cases.description: A 2023 cosmological model challenges the widely accepted Planck satellite age estimate of the universe.
cases.rationale: The established 13.77-billion-year estimate from Planck data directly conflicts with a newer 26.7-billion-year proposal, representing a fundamental disagreement about cosmological models and measurement interpretation.

cases.query: Can employers monitor employees' personal devices used for work?
contexts: The 2018 EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) Article 6 permits employers to process employee data, including device monitoring, when there is a legitimate business interest, provided employees are informed and the monitoring is proportionate.

A January 2024 ruling by the European Court of Human Rights in Lopez Ribalda v. Spain established that covert monitoring of employees, even on work devices, violates Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights unless strictly necessary and pre-authorized by a judicial body.

The French CNIL issued updated guidance in March 2024 stating that any employer monitoring of personal devices used in BYOD arrangements requires explicit, freely given consent that cannot be a condition of employment.
cases.description: Recent court rulings and regulatory guidance restrict the employer monitoring latitude previously allowed under GDPR.
cases.rationale: GDPR's 2018 framework allowed monitoring under legitimate interest, but the 2024 ECHR ruling and CNIL guidance impose stricter consent and necessity requirements, creating a temporal conflict in the legal landscape.

cases.query: Is non-compete enforcement legal for low-wage workers in the United States?
contexts: Under common law principles reaffirmed by many state courts through 2020, non-compete agreements are generally enforceable if they are reasonable in scope, duration, and geographic area, regardless of the worker's wage level.

The FTC's April 2024 final rule bans virtually all non-compete clauses nationwide, with limited exceptions for senior executives earning above $151,164 annually, effectively making non-competes illegal for low-wage workers.
cases.description: FTC's 2024 non-compete ban conflicts with longstanding common law enforcement tradition.
cases.rationale: State courts have historically enforced reasonable non-competes at all wage levels, but the FTC's 2024 rule effectively bans them for low-wage workers, creating a direct temporal conflict between established precedent and new federal regulation.

cases.query: Should healthy adults take a daily aspirin to prevent heart attacks?
contexts: The 2016 U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendation stated that low-dose aspirin (81 mg) is beneficial for adults aged 50-59 with a 10% or greater 10-year cardiovascular risk, receiving a B-grade recommendation.

The USPSTF's updated 2022 recommendation reversed its position, stating that the evidence no longer supports routine aspirin use for primary prevention in adults over 60, and that the decision for adults 40-59 should be individual, downgrading to a C-grade recommendation due to bleeding risks.
cases.description: USPSTF reversed its own aspirin recommendation within six years based on new bleeding risk evidence.
cases.rationale: The same authoritative body (USPSTF) gave a B-grade recommendation for aspirin in 2016 but then effectively reversed it in 2022, with the updated guidance citing bleeding risks that outweigh cardiovascular benefits for most healthy adults.

cases.query: Is vaping a safe alternative to cigarettes for smoking cessation?
contexts: Public Health England's 2018 evidence review concluded that e-cigarettes are approximately 95% less harmful than combustible cigarettes and should be promoted as a cessation tool, recommending that NHS stop-smoking services offer vaping support.

A 2024 WHO technical report found that e-cigarettes contain at least 2,000 chemicals, including known carcinogens like formaldehyde and acrolein, and stated there is insufficient evidence that they aid cessation, recommending that countries ban or strictly regulate them.
cases.description: WHO's 2024 position on e-cigarette safety directly contradicts Public Health England's 2018 endorsement.
cases.rationale: PHE's 2018 report endorsed vaping as 95% safer and a cessation aid, while WHO's 2024 report highlights thousands of harmful chemicals and insufficient cessation evidence, representing a stark temporal disagreement between major health authorities.

cases.query: Is blockchain technology suitable for enterprise supply chain management?
contexts: Gartner's 2019 Hype Cycle report predicted that blockchain would reach mainstream enterprise adoption within 5-10 years, citing pilot programs at Walmart, Maersk, and De Beers as evidence that supply chain transparency use cases were near production-ready.

Gartner's 2024 updated analysis found that 80% of enterprise blockchain supply chain projects launched between 2018 and 2022 were abandoned or mothballed, with most organizations reverting to centralized databases, citing scalability limitations, interoperability failures, and governance complexities.
cases.description: Gartner's own enterprise blockchain predictions from 2019 were contradicted by their 2024 adoption data.
cases.rationale: The same analyst firm predicted mainstream blockchain adoption for supply chains in 2019, but their 2024 data shows 80% of those projects failed, creating a temporal conflict about blockchain's enterprise viability.

cases.query: Is quantum computing a near-term threat to current encryption standards?
contexts: The National Security Agency's 2021 cybersecurity advisory stated that quantum computers capable of breaking RSA-2048 encryption were at least 20-30 years away, and recommended organizations begin planning for post-quantum migration on a gradual timeline.

IBM's December 2023 Quantum Development Roadmap announced achieving a 1,121-qubit processor and projected reaching 100,000 logical qubits by 2033, with cryptographically relevant quantum computing potentially achievable within 10 years, prompting NIST to accelerate its post-quantum cryptography standardization to 2024.
cases.description: IBM's 2023 quantum roadmap challenges NSA's 2021 assessment of the timeline for encryption-breaking quantum computers.
cases.rationale: The NSA estimated 20-30 years in 2021, but IBM's 2023 hardware advances and NIST's accelerated standardization suggest the threat may materialize within 10 years, creating a significant temporal conflict on quantum computing timelines.

cases.query: Are index funds always the best investment strategy for retail investors?
contexts: The 2019 S&P SPIVA Scorecard showed that over 15 years, 92.2% of large-cap active fund managers underperformed the S&P 500 after fees, strongly supporting passive index investing as the optimal strategy for most retail investors.

A 2024 Morningstar analysis found that during the 2022-2023 period of rising interest rates and sector rotation, 55% of active large-cap managers outperformed their benchmark index, and that index concentration risk (the top 7 stocks representing 30% of the S&P 500) introduced systematic risk that active managers could avoid.
cases.description: Recent active management outperformance challenges the long-standing dominance of passive index funds.
cases.rationale: The 2019 SPIVA data overwhelmingly favored index funds over 15 years, but the 2024 Morningstar analysis shows active managers outperformed during recent market stress and highlights concentration risk in indices, creating a temporal conflict about optimal investment strategy.

cases.query: Is cryptocurrency a viable store of value?
contexts: A 2021 Goldman Sachs research note argued that Bitcoin's extreme volatility (annualized at 80%), lack of intrinsic yield, and correlation with risk assets during market stress made it unsuitable as a store of value, recommending clients avoid allocation.

BlackRock's January 2024 Bitcoin ETF filing and subsequent SEC approval argued that Bitcoin had matured as a store of value, citing declining volatility (annualized at 45% in 2023), institutional custody solutions, and its 15-year track record of outperforming gold and equities on a risk-adjusted basis over rolling 4-year periods.
cases.description: BlackRock's 2024 Bitcoin ETF thesis contradicts Goldman Sachs' 2021 rejection of Bitcoin as a store of value.
cases.rationale: Goldman Sachs dismissed Bitcoin's store-of-value potential in 2021 citing 80% volatility, while BlackRock's 2024 ETF filing argues Bitcoin has matured with lower volatility at 45% and superior risk-adjusted returns, representing conflicting assessments from major financial institutions across time.

cases.query: Can the Mars rover complete its extended mission objectives?
contexts: NASA's Perseverance rover has been operating on Mars for over 1,200 sols and its nuclear power source (MMRTG) is designed to provide at least 110 watts for 14 Earth years.
The extended mission plan requires the rover to traverse 28 kilometers of terrain with elevation changes exceeding 600 meters to reach the Jezero crater rim sampling sites.
Engineering telemetry shows the rover's left front wheel has sustained 62% tread degradation after covering only 18 kilometers on relatively flat terrain.
Mission scientists estimate the remaining sampling campaign requires a minimum of 45 operational wheel-kilometers.
cases.description: Power supply is sufficient but wheel degradation rate implies mechanical failure before mission completion.
cases.rationale: The power source supports 14 years of operation, but the wheel has lost 62% tread in 18 km, while the mission needs 45 more km on harder terrain -- implying the rover may not physically survive to use its ample power supply.

cases.query: Can the defendant's confession be used as evidence at trial?
contexts: The defendant signed a written confession at the police station at 3:47 AM on October 12, admitting to the robbery in detail.
Police body camera footage shows officers arrived at the defendant's home at 11:15 PM on October 11 and immediately placed him in handcuffs.
The booking record indicates the defendant was formally read his Miranda rights at 3:30 AM on October 12, seventeen minutes before signing the confession.
The defendant has no prior criminal record and speaks English as a second language with limited proficiency.
cases.description: Confession was signed after Miranda rights were read, but defendant was restrained for over four hours before that.
cases.rationale: While Miranda rights were technically administered before the confession, the 4+ hour custodial detention without rights notification, combined with the suspect's limited English proficiency, implicitly contradicts the voluntariness of the confession.

cases.query: Is TechVenture Inc. a good investment based on its latest earnings report?
contexts: TechVenture Inc. reported Q4 revenue of $2.3 billion, beating analyst estimates of $2.1 billion by 9.5%, marking the eighth consecutive quarter of revenue beats.
The company announced a $500 million stock buyback program and raised its 2025 revenue guidance by 12% to $10.5 billion.
The CFO sold 85% of her vested stock options, totaling $14.2 million, during a pre-announced 10b5-1 trading window that opened three days after the earnings release.
Three independent board members also filed Form 4 disclosures showing combined sales of $8.7 million in the same window.
cases.description: Strong earnings and raised guidance conflict with massive insider selling by the CFO and board members.
cases.rationale: The company beat estimates and raised guidance, which signals confidence, but the CFO selling 85% of her options and board members unloading $8.7M implicitly contradicts the bullish narrative -- insiders are acting as if the stock is overvalued despite publicly optimistic signals.

cases.query: Has the school district's new literacy program improved reading outcomes?
contexts: The Greenfield School District reported that average 3rd-grade reading scores on the state standardized test increased from 62% to 71% proficiency after one year of implementing the Foundations First phonics curriculum.
The district also reported that 15% of students were reclassified from special education reading services to general education during the same year.
State records show the district's 3rd-grade enrollment dropped from 2,400 to 1,950 students between the two testing years, with the superintendent citing 'families relocating due to housing costs.'
The neighboring district, which absorbed many of Greenfield's transferring families, saw its 3rd-grade reading proficiency drop from 68% to 59% in the same period.
cases.description: Reading scores improved but enrollment dropped significantly, and the receiving district's scores declined.
cases.rationale: The 9-point proficiency gain and special education reclassifications look positive, but losing 450 students (19%) while the receiving district's scores dropped by 9 points implicitly suggests the improvement came from lower-performing students leaving rather than from the new curriculum.

cases.query: Is Pluto a planet?
contexts: The International Astronomical Union's 2006 Resolution 5A formally reclassified Pluto as a 'dwarf planet' because it has not cleared its orbital neighborhood of other debris, failing one of three criteria for full planet status.

NASA administrator Jim Bridenstine stated in 2019: 'I am here to tell you, as the NASA administrator, I believe Pluto is a planet,' arguing that the IAU definition is arbitrary and that geological complexity should be the primary criterion.
A 2022 petition signed by over 300 planetary scientists called for reinstating Pluto's planet status, citing that the 'clearing the neighborhood' criterion would also disqualify Earth and Jupiter.
cases.description: The IAU says Pluto is not a planet, but NASA's administrator and hundreds of scientists disagree.
cases.rationale: The IAU formally declassified Pluto in 2006, but NASA's own administrator and 300+ scientists dispute the definition itself, creating a binary yes/no conflict backed by credible authorities on both sides.

cases.query: Can an employer fire an employee for off-duty marijuana use in a legal state?
contexts: Under federal law, marijuana remains a Schedule I controlled substance, and the Drug-Free Workplace Act of 1988 permits employers receiving federal contracts to terminate employees who test positive for THC regardless of state legalization.

California's AB 2188, effective January 2024, prohibits employers from discriminating against employees for off-duty cannabis use and bars the use of THC metabolite tests (which detect past use) in employment decisions, with exceptions only for federal contractors and safety-sensitive positions.
cases.description: Federal law permits termination for marijuana use while California state law prohibits it.
cases.rationale: Federal law explicitly allows firing for THC-positive tests, while California AB 2188 explicitly prohibits discrimination for off-duty use -- a direct binary conflict between federal and state law for non-federal-contractor employers.

cases.query: Is it legal to record a phone conversation without the other party's consent?
contexts: Under federal law (18 U.S.C. 2511), the United States follows a one-party consent rule: recording a phone call is legal as long as one participant (including the person recording) consents, and no court order is required.

California Penal Code Section 632 requires all-party consent for recording confidential communications, making it a criminal offense punishable by a fine of up to $2,500 and up to one year in jail to record a call without the other party's knowledge.
cases.description: Federal law allows one-party consent recording while California law criminalizes it.
cases.rationale: Federal statute says yes (one-party consent is sufficient), California statute says no (all parties must consent) -- a direct binary legal conflict depending on which jurisdiction's law applies.

cases.query: Should you feed a cold and starve a fever?
contexts: A 2002 study by Dutch researchers at the Academic Medical Center in Amsterdam found that eating stimulated the immune response needed to fight viral infections (colds), while fasting activated the immune response needed to fight bacterial infections (fevers), providing scientific support for the adage.

The American College of Physicians and Harvard Medical School's 2023 patient guidance states that adequate nutrition and hydration are essential during any illness, that caloric restriction during fever can impair immune function and delay recovery, and that there is no clinical evidence supporting dietary restriction based on symptom type.
cases.description: A peer-reviewed study supports the folk wisdom while major medical institutions reject it entirely.
cases.rationale: The 2002 Amsterdam study found scientific support for differentiated eating based on illness type, but the ACP and Harvard 2023 guidance directly rejects caloric restriction during fever as harmful -- a binary conflict between a research finding and clinical consensus.
context_sources: Dutch researchers at the Academic Medical Center Research Study (2023)

cases.query: Is sitting for long periods as dangerous as smoking?
contexts: A 2014 meta-analysis published in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute, analyzing 43 studies covering 4 million participants, found that prolonged sitting increased cancer risk by 24%, heart disease mortality by 18%, and all-cause mortality by 24%, leading lead author Dr. Daniela Schmid to call sitting 'the new smoking.'

A 2024 rebuttal published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine by Professor Terry Boyle of the University of South Australia argues that the comparison is 'scientifically inaccurate and harmful,' noting that smoking causes 7 million deaths annually versus an estimated 400,000 attributable to sedentary behavior, and that the risks are not comparable in magnitude, mechanism, or dose-response relationship.
cases.description: One major study equates sitting risks to smoking while another rejects the comparison as grossly misleading.
cases.rationale: The 2014 meta-analysis found sitting increased mortality by 24% and called it 'the new smoking,' but the 2024 rebuttal argues the comparison is inaccurate since smoking kills 17x more people -- a binary conflict about whether the equivalence is valid.
context_sources: Professor Terry Boyle of the University Report (2024)

cases.query: Does static stretching before exercise prevent injuries?
contexts: The American College of Sports Medicine's 2018 guidelines recommend pre-exercise static stretching as part of a comprehensive warm-up routine, citing evidence that it improves range of motion and may reduce the incidence of muscle strains and joint injuries.

A 2021 systematic review in the British Medical Journal covering 12 randomized controlled trials with 8,806 participants concluded that pre-exercise static stretching does not reduce overall injury risk, and may actually impair performance by reducing muscle force production by 5-8% and decreasing vertical jump height.
cases.description: ACSM recommends pre-exercise static stretching while a BMJ systematic review says it does not prevent injuries.
cases.rationale: ACSM guidelines endorse static stretching for injury prevention, but a BMJ systematic review of 12 RCTs finds no injury reduction and 5-8% performance impairment -- directly opposite conclusions on whether the practice is beneficial.

cases.query: Should youth athletes specialize in a single sport early?
contexts: USA Hockey's long-term athlete development model recommends early sport specialization beginning at age 10-12 for competitive-track athletes, arguing that the 10,000-hour rule requires early focused training to develop elite-level skills before physical maturation windows close.

The American Academy of Pediatrics' 2023 clinical report on youth sports recommends against single-sport specialization before age 15-16, citing evidence that early specializers have 81% higher overuse injury rates, 36% higher burnout rates, and are no more likely to reach elite levels than multi-sport athletes.
cases.description: A major sports federation recommends early specialization while the AAP advises against it.
cases.rationale: USA Hockey says specialize by age 10-12 citing skill development windows, while the AAP says wait until 15-16 citing 81% higher injury rates and no elite advantage -- a direct binary conflict between sports development and medical organizations.

cases.query: Is dark mode better for your eyes?
contexts: A 2023 study by the University of Tubingen's Institute for Ophthalmic Research found that reading in dark mode reduced eye strain markers by 22% in a controlled trial of 120 participants who used screens for 6+ hours daily, with participants reporting less visual fatigue and fewer headaches.

Researchers at the University of British Columbia published a 2024 study in the Journal of Experimental Psychology showing that dark mode actually reduces reading comprehension by 11% and increases error rates by 14%, and found no measurable difference in eye strain biomarkers between light and dark modes using objective pupillometry.
cases.description: One study shows dark mode reduces eye strain while another finds no objective benefit and reduced comprehension.
cases.rationale: The Tubingen study found 22% less eye strain with dark mode, while the UBC study found no objective strain difference and 11% worse reading comprehension -- directly conflicting findings on whether dark mode helps or hinders.
context_sources: Journal of Experimental Psychology Research Study (2024)

cases.query: Does using a VPN make you anonymous online?
contexts: ExpressVPN's independent audit conducted by PricewaterhouseCoopers in 2023 confirmed that its TrustedServer technology stores no user logs, runs entirely in RAM, and that even a government subpoena cannot retrieve user browsing data, supporting its claim that VPN users are effectively anonymous.

The Electronic Frontier Foundation's 2024 technical analysis states that VPNs do not provide anonymity because browser fingerprinting, DNS leaks, WebRTC leaks, and traffic correlation attacks can identify users even through a VPN connection, and that at least 26 VPN providers claiming 'no-log' policies were found to retain identifiable user data when subpoenaed.
cases.description: A VPN provider's audit claims effective anonymity while the EFF says VPNs fundamentally cannot provide it.
cases.rationale: ExpressVPN's PwC audit confirms no-log anonymity, while the EFF argues VPNs cannot provide anonymity due to fingerprinting, leak vectors, and documented cases of 'no-log' providers retaining data -- a binary conflict about whether VPN anonymity is real.

cases.query: Is the decline of insect populations a crisis?
contexts: A 2019 global meta-analysis in Biological Conservation found that 40% of insect species are declining, with total insect biomass decreasing by 2.5% per year, and warned of a potential 'insect apocalypse' within decades that could collapse pollination networks and food webs.

A 2023 reanalysis of the same underlying datasets published in Nature Ecology & Evolution found that while certain insect groups (butterflies, beetles) are declining, freshwater insects have increased by 11% since 1990, and that the '40% declining' figure was inflated by geographic bias toward Western European studies, calling the apocalypse framing 'not supported by the totality of evidence.'
cases.description: Same insect data interpreted as either an impending ecological apocalypse or a geographically biased exaggeration.
cases.rationale: Both analyses reference overlapping datasets but draw opposite conclusions: one sees a 2.5% annual decline as catastrophic, the other identifies geographic bias and rising freshwater insect populations as evidence against the crisis narrative.

cases.query: Does the discovery of phosphine on Venus indicate extraterrestrial life?
contexts: A 2020 paper in Nature Astronomy by Greaves et al. reported detecting 20 parts per billion of phosphine in Venus's atmosphere using the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope, arguing that no known abiotic chemical process can account for the observed concentration and that a biological source is the most plausible explanation.

A 2022 reanalysis by Villanueva et al. using the same spectral data but different calibration techniques estimated the phosphine concentration at less than 1 part per billion, well within the range explainable by volcanic activity and photochemistry, and concluded that the detection does not require a biological explanation.
cases.description: Same spectral data from Venus interpreted as either evidence for life or an artifact of calibration error.
cases.rationale: Greaves et al. interpret the spectral signal as 20 ppb phosphine requiring biological origin, while Villanueva et al. reanalyze the same data and find less than 1 ppb explainable by geology -- same data, opposite interpretations about extraterrestrial life.

cases.query: Is the economy recovering?
contexts: The Bureau of Economic Analysis reported that U.S. GDP grew 2.1% in Q3 2024, unemployment fell to 3.8%, consumer spending rose 1.5%, and the economy added 254,000 jobs in September, marking the 33rd consecutive month of job gains.

Analysis by the Economic Policy Institute using the same government data notes that real wages declined 0.4% year-over-year when adjusted for housing costs, household debt reached a record $17.7 trillion, the growth was driven primarily by a 4.6% increase in government spending, and the labor force participation rate remained 0.8 points below pre-pandemic levels.
cases.description: Same economic data interpreted as either a strong recovery or a fragile expansion masking structural weakness.
cases.rationale: The headline numbers (GDP up, unemployment down, jobs added) suggest recovery, but the same data reframed (declining real wages, record debt, government-driven growth, low participation) suggests underlying weakness -- identical facts supporting opposite conclusions.

cases.query: Is the housing market overvalued?
contexts: The National Association of Realtors' 2024 Q3 report highlights that median home prices rose 4.2% year-over-year to $412,300, existing home inventory reached its highest level in 3 years at 4.2 months of supply, and mortgage rates at 6.8% are stabilizing, characterizing the market as 'normalizing toward sustainable growth.'

An analysis by the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas using the same price and income data calculates that the price-to-income ratio reached 7.1x in Q3 2024, exceeding the 2006 pre-crisis peak of 6.8x, that the 4.2 months of inventory represents a 58% increase from the prior year signaling weakening demand, and that affordability for first-time buyers has reached its lowest point since 1984.
cases.description: Same housing data interpreted as healthy normalization by one source and pre-crisis overvaluation by another.
cases.rationale: NAR interprets rising prices and increased inventory as normalization, while the Dallas Fed interprets the same metrics as price-to-income exceeding 2006 levels and historic unaffordability -- identical data framed as either stability or a bubble.

cases.query: Are ultra-processed foods responsible for the obesity epidemic?
contexts: A 2024 Lancet study analyzing dietary data from 197 countries found that ultra-processed food consumption increased by 48% globally between 2000 and 2020, correlating with a 65% increase in obesity rates, and concluded that ultra-processed foods are 'the primary dietary driver of the global obesity epidemic.'

Nutrition researchers at the University of Cambridge published a 2024 rebuttal in the BMJ arguing that the correlation is confounded by sedentary lifestyles, increased portion sizes, and urbanization occurring over the same period, and that controlled metabolic ward studies show calorie-matched diets of processed and unprocessed foods produce identical weight outcomes when total calories are controlled.
cases.description: Same global trend data interpreted as proof of ultra-processed food harm or as a confounded correlation.
cases.rationale: The Lancet study interprets the parallel rise in processed food consumption and obesity as causal, while Cambridge researchers argue the correlation is confounded and that calorie-controlled studies show processing itself does not cause weight gain -- same data, conflicting causal interpretations.
context_sources: Center for Science in the Public Interest (2024)

cases.query: Does moderate alcohol consumption have health benefits?
contexts: A 2022 observational study in JAMA Network Open analyzing 371,463 UK Biobank participants found that moderate drinkers (7-14 drinks/week) had 14% lower all-cause mortality than non-drinkers, with the strongest protective association for cardiovascular death, consistent with decades of J-curve epidemiological findings.

A 2023 meta-analysis in JAMA by Dr. Tim Stockwell re-examined 107 studies including the UK Biobank data and found that after correcting for 'abstainer bias' (former drinkers and ill people in the non-drinker reference group), the apparent protective effect disappeared entirely, with even light drinking associated with slightly increased mortality.
cases.description: Same cohort data shows either protective effects of moderate drinking or an artifact of flawed reference groups.
cases.rationale: The 2022 study finds a 14% mortality benefit for moderate drinkers, but the 2023 meta-analysis reanalyzes overlapping data and argues the benefit vanishes when the non-drinker control group is corrected for abstainer bias -- same data, opposite health conclusions.

cases.query: Has No Child Left Behind improved American education?
contexts: NAEP data from 2002 to 2013 shows that 4th-grade math scores increased by 11 points and 8th-grade math scores by 9 points nationally, with Black and Hispanic students showing gains of 14 and 16 points respectively, narrowing the achievement gap by 8-10 points during the NCLB era.

Analysis by the Brookings Institution of the same NAEP data notes that the rate of improvement actually slowed during NCLB compared to the pre-NCLB period of 1996-2002, that reading scores showed no significant gains, that gains were concentrated in low-stakes 4th-grade assessments, and that 12th-grade scores remained flat, suggesting the improvements reflected test preparation rather than genuine learning.
cases.description: Same NAEP test data interpreted as evidence that NCLB narrowed gaps or merely produced test-prep artifacts.
cases.rationale: The raw NAEP data shows 11-point math gains and gap narrowing, but reanalysis of the same data shows gains slowed relative to pre-NCLB trends, were absent in reading, and did not reach 12th grade -- identical data supporting opposite conclusions about policy effectiveness.

cases.query: Do charter schools outperform traditional public schools?
contexts: Stanford University's CREDO 2023 national study of 2.7 million charter school students found they gained the equivalent of 16 additional days of learning in reading and 6 days in math per year compared to matched peers in traditional public schools, with urban charter students gaining 40 additional reading days.

The National Education Policy Center at the University of Colorado reviewed the same CREDO data and argued that 16 extra days (4% of the school year) is educationally negligible, that the matching methodology fails to account for selection bias from motivated families, that 37% of charters performed worse than traditional schools, and that the urban gains are driven by a handful of high-performing networks like KIPP and Success Academy that serve only 3% of charter students.
cases.description: Same CREDO dataset interpreted as demonstrating charter school superiority or as showing negligible, uneven results.
cases.rationale: CREDO's data shows 16 extra learning days for charter students, but reinterpretation of the same data frames this as a trivial 4% difference driven by selection bias and a few elite networks, with 37% of charters actually underperforming -- identical data, opposite policy conclusions.

cases.query: Did immigration increase or decrease crime rates in the United States in the 2010s?
contexts: FBI Uniform Crime Report data shows that between 2010 and 2020, the foreign-born population in the United States increased by 4.3 million while violent crime rates fell 15% and property crime rates fell 25%, consistent with peer-reviewed studies finding immigrants commit crimes at lower rates than native-born citizens.

The Federation for American Immigration Reform analyzed the same FBI crime data alongside ICE enforcement records and found that non-citizen arrests for drug offenses increased 42%, that border counties experienced a 17% increase in aggravated assaults, and that the decline in national crime rates was driven by demographic and policing changes unrelated to immigration patterns.
cases.description: Same FBI crime data interpreted as showing immigration reduces crime or as masking localized crime increases.
cases.rationale: National FBI data shows crime falling as immigration rose, but disaggregated analysis of the same data highlights rising drug arrests and border county assaults, with the national decline attributed to other factors -- identical datasets supporting opposite conclusions about immigration's effect on crime.

cases.query: Has remote voting (vote-by-mail) increased election fraud?
contexts: The Heritage Foundation's election fraud database documents 1,465 proven cases of voter fraud across the United States since 2000, with mail-in ballot fraud comprising 24% of all cases, and argues this represents a 'significant and growing threat' to election integrity as mail voting expanded after 2020.

The Brennan Center for Justice analyzed the same Heritage database and noted that 1,465 cases across 24 years and billions of ballots cast represents a fraud rate of 0.00006%, that mail ballot fraud declined from 0.00004% to 0.00003% even as mail voting doubled between 2016 and 2022, and characterized the fraud threat as 'infinitesimally rare and declining.'
cases.description: Same Heritage fraud database interpreted as showing a growing threat or as proof that fraud is vanishingly rare.
cases.rationale: Heritage presents 1,465 cases and 24% mail-ballot share as a significant threat, while Brennan Center takes the same 1,465 cases and divides by billions of ballots to get 0.00006%, framing it as negligible -- identical data, opposite conclusions about the severity of mail voting fraud.

cases.query: Does intermittent fasting improve cognitive function?
contexts: A 2022 randomized controlled trial at Johns Hopkins University enrolled 200 adults aged 55-75 in a 16:8 intermittent fasting protocol and found that working memory scores improved by 15% and executive function by 11% over 12 weeks compared to controls eating regular meals.

A 2024 pre-registered replication study at the University of Sydney with 500 participants aged 55-75 using the identical 16:8 protocol and cognitive battery found no significant difference in working memory (p=0.71) or executive function (p=0.43) between fasting and control groups over 16 weeks.
cases.description: A well-powered replication study failed to reproduce cognitive benefits of intermittent fasting found in the original trial.
cases.rationale: The Johns Hopkins trial found 15% working memory improvement with intermittent fasting, but the larger Sydney replication with identical protocol found no effect (p=0.71) -- a direct replication failure on the same research question.

cases.query: Does vitamin D supplementation reduce the risk of respiratory infections?
contexts: A 2017 meta-analysis in the BMJ pooling 25 randomized controlled trials with 11,321 participants found that vitamin D supplementation reduced the risk of acute respiratory infections by 12% overall and by 70% in participants with severe deficiency (serum levels below 25 nmol/L).

The VITAL randomized trial published in the BMJ in 2022, enrolling 25,871 participants over 5 years, found no significant reduction in respiratory infections with 2,000 IU daily vitamin D supplementation (HR 0.97, 95% CI 0.93-1.01), including in the subgroup with baseline deficiency.
cases.description: The largest-ever vitamin D respiratory trial contradicted the meta-analytic finding of protective benefit.
cases.rationale: The 2017 meta-analysis of 25 trials found a 12% infection reduction (70% in deficient individuals), but the much larger 2022 VITAL trial of 25,871 people found no benefit even in deficient subgroups -- conflicting results from rigorous studies on the same question.

cases.query: Do statins reduce mortality in elderly patients without prior heart disease?
contexts: The PROSPER trial (2002) enrolled 5,804 patients aged 70-82 with cardiovascular risk factors but no prior heart events and found that pravastatin reduced cardiac events by 19% but showed no reduction in all-cause mortality (HR 0.97, p=0.74) over 3.2 years.

A 2020 Australian study (STAREE pilot data) of 1,800 patients aged 70+ without prior cardiovascular disease found that statin use was associated with a 25% reduction in all-cause mortality and a 35% reduction in cardiovascular events over 4.5 years, leading researchers to conclude that statins provide meaningful survival benefit in healthy elderly populations.
cases.description: One trial finds statins reduce cardiac events but not mortality in the elderly, while another finds a significant mortality benefit.
cases.rationale: PROSPER found no mortality benefit (HR 0.97) for statins in the elderly, while the STAREE pilot data found a 25% mortality reduction in a similar population -- directly conflicting results on whether statins extend life in healthy older adults.

cases.query: Does power posing increase confidence and testosterone levels?
contexts: The original 2010 study by Amy Cuddy and colleagues at Harvard, published in Psychological Science, found that holding expansive 'power poses' for two minutes increased testosterone by 20%, decreased cortisol by 25%, and increased self-reported feelings of power and willingness to take risks in a sample of 42 participants.

A 2017 pre-registered replication by Ranehill et al. published in Psychological Science with 200 participants found no significant effect of power posing on testosterone (p=0.49), cortisol (p=0.35), or risk-taking behavior, and a 2018 P-curve analysis by Simmons and Simonsohn concluded the original study's results were likely false positives driven by researcher degrees of freedom.
cases.description: The famous power posing study's hormonal findings failed to replicate in a larger pre-registered study.
cases.rationale: Cuddy's 2010 study found 20% testosterone increase from power posing, but the 2017 replication with 5x the sample found no hormonal effects (p=0.49) and a P-curve analysis suggested the original was a false positive -- a high-profile replication failure.

cases.query: Does the marshmallow test predict long-term life outcomes?
contexts: Walter Mischel's original 1972 marshmallow test and subsequent follow-ups through 2011 found that children who delayed gratification at age 4 had SAT scores 210 points higher, lower BMI, lower divorce rates, and higher educational attainment decades later, suggesting that early self-control is a powerful predictor of life success.

A 2018 conceptual replication by Watts, Duncan, and Quan published in Psychological Science tested 918 children (10x the original sample) and found that the marshmallow test's predictive power dropped by over 50% when controlling for the child's family socioeconomic status and home environment, and became statistically insignificant for most outcomes when maternal education was included as a covariate.
cases.description: The iconic marshmallow test's predictive power was substantially diminished when a larger study controlled for socioeconomic factors.
cases.rationale: Mischel's studies found a strong link between childhood delay of gratification and life success, but Watts et al. showed the effect dropped 50%+ and became non-significant when controlling for SES -- conflicting conclusions about whether self-control or socioeconomic background drives outcomes.

cases.query: Does unconscious priming influence complex behavior?
contexts: John Bargh's famous 1996 experiment published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology found that participants primed with elderly-related words (Florida, bingo, wrinkle) walked significantly more slowly down a hallway afterward, demonstrating that unconscious semantic priming can influence complex motor behavior.

Doyen et al.'s 2012 direct replication published in PLOS ONE with 120 participants found no effect of elderly priming on walking speed when experimenter expectations were controlled using a double-blind protocol, suggesting the original result was driven by experimenter expectancy effects rather than unconscious priming.
cases.description: The landmark elderly priming study failed to replicate when experimenter expectancy effects were controlled.
cases.rationale: Bargh's 1996 study found elderly-word priming slowed walking speed, but Doyen et al.'s double-blind replication found no effect, attributing the original finding to unblinded experimenters unconsciously influencing participant behavior -- conflicting results on unconscious behavioral priming.
context_sources: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology Research Study (2023)

cases.query: Do artificial sweeteners cause weight gain?
contexts: A 2023 WHO-commissioned systematic review of 56 studies found that long-term use of non-sugar sweeteners was associated with a 76% increased risk of type 2 diabetes, increased BMI, and higher cardiovascular mortality, leading the WHO to recommend against their use for weight control.

A 2024 randomized controlled trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine, following 1,548 overweight adults for 2 years, found that replacing sugary drinks with artificially sweetened alternatives resulted in 5.3 kg average weight loss, improved insulin sensitivity, and no increase in metabolic disease markers, and criticized the WHO review for relying heavily on observational data subject to reverse causation.
cases.description: A WHO review links artificial sweeteners to weight gain and diabetes while a large RCT shows they aid weight loss.
cases.rationale: The WHO review of 56 studies finds 76% increased diabetes risk with artificial sweeteners, but a 2-year RCT of 1,548 adults finds 5.3 kg weight loss and improved insulin sensitivity -- conflicting evidence likely due to the difference between observational and experimental study designs.

cases.query: Does eating red meat increase cancer risk?
contexts: The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), part of the WHO, classified processed meat as a Group 1 carcinogen and red meat as a Group 2A probable carcinogen in 2015, based on a review of 800 epidemiological studies finding that 50g of processed meat daily increases colorectal cancer risk by 18%.

The NutriRECS consortium published a 2019 systematic review in the Annals of Internal Medicine covering 61 studies with 4 million participants and concluded that the evidence linking red and processed meat to cancer is 'low-certainty,' that the absolute risk increase is 'very small' (7 fewer cancer cases per 1,000 people with reduced consumption), and recommended that adults continue current meat consumption levels.
cases.description: IARC classifies red meat as a probable carcinogen while NutriRECS says the evidence is low-certainty and the risk is trivial.
cases.rationale: IARC reviewed 800 studies and classified processed meat as a definite carcinogen, but NutriRECS reviewed 61 studies with 4M participants and called the evidence 'low-certainty' with negligible absolute risk -- same research question, opposing conclusions and dietary recommendations.

cases.query: Are microplastics in drinking water harmful to human health?
contexts: A 2024 study published in the New England Journal of Medicine analyzed carotid artery plaques from 312 patients and found that patients with detectable microplastics in their plaques had a 4.5-fold increased risk of heart attack, stroke, or death over 34 months, providing the first direct evidence linking microplastics to cardiovascular disease in humans.

The WHO's 2023 systematic review of microplastics in drinking water concluded that current levels of microplastic exposure through drinking water 'do not appear to pose a health risk' based on available toxicological evidence, that the concentrations found in tap water are orders of magnitude below levels shown to cause harm in animal studies, and that there is 'no evidence of human health concern' at current exposure levels.
cases.description: A NEJM study links microplastics to cardiovascular death while a WHO review says current exposures pose no health risk.
cases.rationale: The NEJM study found 4.5x increased cardiovascular mortality in patients with microplastics in arterial plaques, but the WHO concluded microplastics in drinking water pose no health risk at current levels -- directly conflicting assessments of microplastic danger to humans.
context_sources: NIH National Institute of Health Study (2024)

cases.query: Is ocean acidification killing coral reefs?
contexts: A 2020 study in Nature Climate Change measuring carbonate chemistry across 22 reef systems found that ocean pH has decreased by 0.1 units since pre-industrial times, causing a 30% reduction in coral calcification rates, and projected that 70% of tropical reefs would experience net dissolution by 2050 under current emission trends.

A 2023 field study published in Science examined coral communities near natural CO2 seeps in Papua New Guinea where pH levels already match 2100 projections, and found thriving coral communities with 85% cover, diverse species composition, and normal calcification rates, suggesting that many reef species can adapt to acidified conditions over generational timescales.
cases.description: One study predicts acidification will dissolve 70% of reefs by 2050 while field observations show reefs thriving at projected pH levels.
cases.rationale: The 2020 Nature study projects catastrophic reef dissolution from acidification, but the 2023 Science field study finds thriving reefs at even lower pH levels near CO2 seeps -- directly conflicting predictions about coral survival under ocean acidification.

cases.query: How much has global sea level risen since 1900?
contexts: The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (2021) states that global mean sea level rose approximately 20 centimeters (0.20 meters) between 1901 and 2018, based on tide gauge records and satellite altimetry data.

A 2023 study by researchers at the University of Siegen published in Nature Communications, using revised satellite calibrations and updated tide gauge corrections, estimates that global sea level rise since 1900 was approximately 28 centimeters (0.28 meters), noting that the IPCC figure underestimates acceleration in recent decades.
cases.description: Two authoritative sources disagree on total sea level rise since 1900 by a 40% margin.
cases.rationale: The IPCC reports 20 cm of sea level rise since 1900, while the 2023 Nature Communications study estimates 28 cm using revised calibrations -- a 40% discrepancy on the same physical measurement, with significant implications for projections.
context_sources: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change Report (2021)
Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change Research Study (2023)

cases.query: How many concussions occur in the NFL each season?
contexts: The NFL's official 2023 injury report stated that there were 174 diagnosed concussions during the regular season and postseason combined, representing a 10% decline from the previous year, attributing the improvement to enhanced helmet safety standards and updated tackling protocols.

A 2024 independent analysis by Boston University's CTE Center, using sideline video review, undiagnosed symptom data from player surveys, and post-career neurological assessments, estimated that the actual concussion count for the same 2023 season was between 450 and 600, noting that approximately 60% of concussions go unreported due to player reluctance, inadequate sideline screening, and the league's Return to Play protocol incentivizing underreporting.
cases.description: The NFL reports 174 concussions while an independent analysis estimates 450-600 for the same season.
cases.rationale: The NFL's official count of 174 concussions is 2.5-3.5x lower than Boston University's estimate of 450-600, representing a fundamental disagreement about the true injury rate with significant player safety implications.

cases.query: How much does the average wedding cost in the United States?
contexts: The Knot's 2024 Real Weddings Study surveyed 12,000 couples across all 50 states and found that the average cost of a wedding in the United States was $35,000. This figure includes the ceremony venue, reception, catering, photography, flowers, entertainment, and wedding planner fees. The report notes that costs have risen approximately 8% from the previous year, driven primarily by increased catering and venue pricing in major metropolitan areas like New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago.

WeddingWire's 2024 Annual Survey, based on self-reported data from 9,500 couples nationwide, reports the national average wedding cost at $27,400. The survey methodology excludes honeymoon expenses and engagement ring purchases but includes all ceremony and reception costs. Regional variation is significant, with couples in the Northeast spending an average of $38,000 while those in the South average $22,000 according to the same dataset. The median cost was lower at $22,500, reflecting the influence of high-cost outliers.
cases.description: Two major wedding industry surveys report substantially different average costs ($35,000 vs $27,400)
cases.rationale: A $7,600 gap between two large surveys of the same year represents a meaningful disagreement about average wedding costs that cannot be reconciled without understanding methodological differences.

cases.query: How many species of birds are there worldwide?
contexts: According to BirdLife International's 2024 State of the World's Birds report, there are approximately 11,188 recognized bird species globally. This count follows the Biological Species Concept, which classifies species based on reproductive isolation. The organization has maintained this taxonomy since 1990 and it is used by the International Union for Conservation of Nature for conservation assessments and Red List classifications.

A comprehensive genomic analysis published in the Proceedings of the Royal Society in 2024 identifies approximately 18,400 bird species worldwide. The researchers applied the phylogenetic species concept, which distinguishes species based on diagnosable genetic and morphological differences. Lead author Dr. Robert Nakamura noted that many populations currently classified as subspecies show sufficient genetic divergence to warrant full species status under this framework.
cases.description: Two authoritative sources give vastly different bird species counts (11,188 vs 18,400) based on different taxonomic concepts
cases.rationale: The 7,200-species gap reflects a fundamental disagreement in classification methodology that should be flagged rather than presenting either number as definitive.

cases.query: What percentage of employees would quit rather than return to the office full-time?
contexts: A Gallup workplace survey conducted in Q1 2025 with 15,000 respondents found that 29% of remote-capable workers would actively seek a new job if their employer eliminated remote work options entirely. The survey also found that 54% of these workers preferred a hybrid arrangement of two to three days in the office per week, suggesting that moderate schedule flexibility satisfies the majority of employees without requiring full remote work.

FlexJobs' 2025 Work Flexibility Report, surveying 8,200 professionals across 14 industries, found that 57% of respondents said they would absolutely look for a new job if forced to return to in-person work full-time. Additionally, 17% said they would quit immediately without having another job lined up. The report emphasized that remote work has become a non-negotiable benefit for the majority of knowledge workers, with the strongest preferences observed among workers aged 35 to 50.
cases.description: Two workplace surveys report very different percentages of employees who would quit over return-to-office mandates (29% vs 57%)
cases.rationale: A near-doubling in the reported percentage (29% vs 57%) represents a significant factual disagreement between two credible surveys that should be flagged.

cases.query: How much water does it take to produce one pound of beef?
contexts: The Water Footprint Network's global assessment calculates that producing one pound of beef requires approximately 1,800 gallons of water when accounting for drinking water, feed crop irrigation, and processing facilities. This figure represents a weighted global average across different farming systems including intensive feedlot operations and extensive grazing systems in various climate zones. The organization describes beef as having the largest water footprint of any common protein source by a significant margin.

Research from the University of California, Davis published in the Journal of Animal Science found that beef production in the western United States requires approximately 410 gallons of water per pound. The study accounted for actual irrigation water consumed, rainfall captured by pastures, and processing water, arguing that previous estimates dramatically overcount by including non-consumptive rainfall that falls on grasslands regardless of whether cattle are present on the land.
cases.description: Two sources give dramatically different water footprints for beef production (1,800 vs 410 gallons per pound)
cases.rationale: A four-fold difference in water usage figures represents a major disagreement that should be flagged, even though methodological differences partially explain the gap.
context_sources: Journal of Animal Science Research Study (2024)

cases.query: What is the failure rate for restaurant businesses in the first year?
contexts: A comprehensive study by Ohio State University analyzing 350,000 restaurant openings from the Bureau of Labor Statistics data found that approximately 60% of restaurants close within the first year of operation. The study attributed high failure rates to undercapitalization, poor location selection, and inadequate market research. Restaurants in urban areas showed slightly higher failure rates at 64% compared to 55% in suburban locations.

The National Restaurant Association's 2024 Industry Factbook reports that approximately 17% of restaurants close within their first year, based on IRS tax filing cessation data. The NRA notes that the restaurant industry's first-year closure rate is comparable to other small business sectors. The association emphasizes that popular claims of 60-90% failure rates conflate temporary closures, ownership transfers, and rebranding with actual business failures.
cases.description: Two sources report vastly different restaurant first-year failure rates (60% vs 17%)
cases.rationale: The enormous gap between 60% and 17% represents a direct factual disagreement that should be clearly flagged rather than presenting either figure as authoritative.

cases.query: How many people in the US are affected by food insecurity?
contexts: The USDA's annual Household Food Security report for 2024 found that 33.1 million Americans lived in food-insecure households, representing approximately 10.2% of the total U.S. population. This figure uses the USDA's standardized 18-item survey instrument measuring food access and availability over the previous 12 months. The rate decreased slightly from 10.5% the prior year, continuing a downward trend attributed to expanded federal nutrition assistance programs.

Feeding America's Map the Meal Gap 2024 study estimates that 47 million people in the United States experience food insecurity, including 14 million children under the age of 18. The nonprofit's methodology incorporates USDA data alongside local unemployment rates, poverty indicators, housing cost burdens, and food price indexes at the county level to model food insecurity more comprehensively than the narrower federal household survey captures.
cases.description: Federal data and nonprofit analysis give substantially different food insecurity figures (33.1 million vs 47 million)
cases.rationale: A 14-million-person gap between two authoritative sources on the same social issue represents a significant disagreement that should be flagged.
context_sources: U.S. Department of Agriculture Research Study (2024)

cases.query: What is the average salary for a data scientist in the United States?
contexts: Glassdoor's 2025 salary data, based on 48,000 self-reported compensation entries from verified employees, shows the average data scientist salary in the United States is $128,500 per year. The median base salary is $121,000 with an additional $15,000 in annual bonuses and stock compensation. Senior data scientists average $162,000 in total compensation, and entry-level data scientists earn approximately $95,000 according to the platform's employer-reported figures.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics program for May 2024 reports the mean annual wage for data scientists at $108,020. The median annual wage is $103,500, with the lowest 10% of earners receiving below $61,400 and the highest 10% earning above $174,500. BLS data is derived from employer payroll records submitted through mandatory surveys covering approximately 1.1 million business establishments nationwide, providing what the agency considers the most representative compensation data available.
cases.description: Two salary data sources report different average data scientist salaries ($128,500 vs $108,020)
cases.rationale: A $20,000 gap between two widely-cited salary databases represents a meaningful disagreement that should be flagged when answering salary questions.

cases.query: Does intermittent fasting help with weight loss?
contexts: A 12-month randomized controlled trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2024, involving 550 participants, found that intermittent fasting produced significantly greater weight loss than traditional calorie restriction. Participants following a 16:8 fasting protocol lost an average of 14.2 pounds compared to 8.1 pounds in the calorie-restriction group. The fasting group also showed improved insulin sensitivity and reduced inflammatory markers.

A meta-analysis of 27 clinical trials published in the Journal of the American Medical Association in 2025 concluded that intermittent fasting offers no meaningful weight loss advantage over standard calorie reduction. Lead author Dr. Patricia Holden stated that when total caloric intake is matched, fasting protocols produce nearly identical outcomes. The analysis found an average difference of only 0.7 pounds between fasting and non-fasting groups over 12 months.
cases.description: One study finds intermittent fasting significantly better for weight loss, while a meta-analysis finds no meaningful advantage
cases.rationale: A single large RCT claims significant benefit while a meta-analysis of 27 trials finds effectively no difference, representing a direct contradiction in conclusions.

cases.query: Is year-round schooling better for student achievement?
contexts: A longitudinal study by the National Education Policy Center tracking 42,000 students across 180 schools found that year-round schooling significantly improves academic outcomes. Students in year-round programs scored 11 percentile points higher on standardized math tests and 8 points higher in reading compared to peers on traditional calendars. The benefits were most pronounced for low-income students who experienced less summer learning loss.

Research published in the Review of Educational Research by Dr. Harris Cooper and colleagues analyzed 39 studies of year-round schooling and concluded that it has no significant effect on student achievement. The meta-analysis found that initial gains attributed to year-round calendars disappear when controlling for selection bias and socioeconomic factors. Schools that adopted year-round schedules tended to receive additional funding and resources that confounded the results.
cases.description: One study finds year-round schooling significantly improves achievement while another finds no significant effect
cases.rationale: Direct opposition between a positive finding (11 percentile point improvement) and a meta-analysis finding no effect when controlling for confounds.
context_sources: National Education Policy Center Research Study (2023)

cases.query: Should homeowners invest in solar panels based on financial return?
contexts: An analysis by EnergySage based on 2024 installation data from 35,000 homeowners found that residential solar panels provide an average return on investment of 10-15% annually, with most systems paying for themselves within 6-8 years. After the payback period, homeowners save an average of $1,500 per year on electricity bills. Federal tax credits covering 30% of installation costs significantly improve the financial case.

A study by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory published in Nature Energy found that the financial returns of residential solar are frequently overstated. After accounting for actual degradation rates, maintenance costs, insurance increases, and the opportunity cost of capital, the effective ROI drops to 2-4% annually for most homeowners. The study also found that 23% of systems failed to pay for themselves within their 25-year warranty period due to unexpectedly low energy production.
cases.description: One source claims solar panels provide 10-15% annual ROI while another finds only 2-4% after full cost accounting
cases.rationale: A five-fold difference in claimed ROI (10-15% vs 2-4%) represents a direct contradiction in financial conclusions about the same investment.

cases.query: Is organic produce healthier than conventionally grown produce?
contexts: A systematic review published in the British Journal of Nutrition analyzed 343 peer-reviewed studies and concluded that organic crops have significantly higher concentrations of antioxidants, with 18-69% more polyphenols compared to conventional crops. The review also found that organic produce contains 48% lower cadmium concentrations and significantly fewer pesticide residues. The authors concluded these differences are nutritionally meaningful and relevant to human health.

Stanford University's Annals of Internal Medicine review of 237 studies found no strong evidence that organic foods are significantly more nutritious than conventional alternatives. While organic produce had 30% lower pesticide residues, the levels in conventional produce were almost always within safety limits. The researchers found no clinically meaningful differences in vitamin or mineral content and concluded that consuming organic food does not produce measurable health benefits.
cases.description: One systematic review finds organic produce significantly healthier while another finds no meaningful health benefit
cases.rationale: Two large systematic reviews reach opposite conclusions about whether organic food's nutritional differences translate to actual health benefits.

cases.query: Does increasing the minimum wage reduce employment?
contexts: A widely cited study by economists at the University of Washington analyzing Seattle's minimum wage increase to $15 per hour found that the policy reduced total hours worked in low-wage jobs by 9.4%, resulting in a net income loss of $125 per month for affected workers. The study used administrative payroll data covering 90% of Washington state workers and found that employers cut hours significantly in response to the wage increase.

Research by economists at the University of California, Berkeley, studying the same Seattle minimum wage increase, found no significant reduction in employment or hours worked in the restaurant sector. Using a border discontinuity design comparing Seattle restaurants to those in neighboring suburbs, the study found that wages rose 7% with no measurable job losses. The researchers attributed the difference to their methodology better controlling for economic trends.
cases.description: Two studies of the same minimum wage increase reach opposite conclusions about its employment effects
cases.rationale: Using the same policy event, one study finds significant job losses while the other finds none, representing a direct empirical contradiction.

cases.query: Is it legal to record a phone call without the other party's consent in California?
contexts: California Penal Code Section 632 requires all-party consent for recording confidential phone conversations. A 2024 ruling by the California Court of Appeal in Martinez v. TeleCorp reaffirmed that recording a phone call without the consent of all parties is a criminal offense punishable by a fine of up to $2,500 per violation or imprisonment for up to one year. The court emphasized that this applies to both personal and business calls.

The National Conference of State Legislatures' 2024 guide on recording laws states that California is a one-party consent state for phone recordings, meaning only one participant needs to consent to the recording. The guide notes that California follows the federal Wiretap Act standard, which permits recording as long as at least one party to the conversation has given consent. The NCSL classifies 38 states as one-party consent jurisdictions.
cases.description: One source says California requires all-party consent for recording while another classifies it as one-party consent
cases.rationale: These sources directly contradict each other on a binary legal question: California is either all-party or one-party consent. Both cannot be correct.

cases.query: Does cracking your knuckles cause arthritis?
contexts: A study published in the Journal of the American Board of Family Medicine in 2024 followed 215 habitual knuckle crackers and 210 non-crackers over a 15-year period. The research found that habitual knuckle cracking was associated with a statistically significant increase in hand osteoarthritis, with crackers showing 2.3 times higher rates of joint cartilage deterioration on MRI imaging. The study's lead author recommended patients avoid the habit.

The Arthritis Foundation states definitively that cracking your knuckles does not cause arthritis. This position is supported by a comprehensive meta-analysis in Arthritis & Rheumatology reviewing 11 studies with over 4,000 participants that found no association between habitual knuckle cracking and joint inflammation or arthritis development. Dr. Donald Unger's famous self-experiment, cracking only his left hand for 60 years, showed no difference in arthritis between hands.
cases.description: One study links knuckle cracking to arthritis while the Arthritis Foundation and a meta-analysis say it does not cause arthritis
cases.rationale: A direct yes-or-no contradiction: one source finds a significant association while another authoritatively denies any connection.

cases.query: Is homework beneficial for elementary school students?
contexts: A 2024 study by Duke University psychologist Dr. Harris Cooper, analyzing 60 research studies on homework effectiveness, found that homework has no measurable academic benefit for students in elementary school (grades K-5). The research showed zero correlation between time spent on homework and standardized test scores or grades for this age group. Cooper recommended that elementary schools eliminate or drastically reduce homework assignments.

The National PTA and National Education Association jointly published a research brief in 2024 supporting homework for all grade levels. Their analysis of longitudinal data from 12,000 elementary students showed that students completing 20-30 minutes of nightly homework scored 7 percentile points higher on end-of-year assessments. The organizations maintained that age-appropriate homework builds study habits, reinforces classroom learning, and develops student responsibility.
cases.description: One study finds homework has no academic benefit for elementary students while education organizations find measurable gains
cases.rationale: Direct binary contradiction: one source finds zero benefit while another finds a 7-percentile-point improvement from elementary homework.
context_sources: National PTA and National Education Association Research Study (2024)

cases.query: Does vitamin D supplementation prevent cancer?
contexts: The VITAL randomized clinical trial, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, followed 25,871 participants for an average of 5.3 years and found that vitamin D supplementation at 2,000 IU daily did not significantly reduce the incidence of invasive cancer compared to placebo. The hazard ratio was 0.96 with a 95% confidence interval spanning 0.88 to 1.06, indicating no statistically significant protective effect.

A pooled analysis of participant-level data from 12 randomized trials published in the Annals of Oncology found that vitamin D supplementation reduced cancer mortality by 13% overall and reduced incidence of metastatic or fatal cancer by 17%. Researchers from Harvard and the German Cancer Research Center reported that the protective effect was most pronounced in participants who maintained serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels above 40 ng/mL throughout the study period.
cases.description: A major RCT finds no cancer prevention benefit from vitamin D while a pooled analysis finds significant mortality reduction
cases.rationale: One large trial finds no benefit while a pooled analysis of multiple trials finds a meaningful 13-17% reduction, directly contradicting each other.
context_sources: New England Journal of Medicine Study (2022)
Harvard and the German Cancer Research Center Research Study (2022)

cases.query: Is remote patient monitoring effective at reducing hospital readmissions?
contexts: A randomized controlled trial conducted by the Veterans Health Administration involving 3,200 heart failure patients found that remote patient monitoring using connected devices reduced 30-day hospital readmission rates by 38% compared to standard care. The monitoring program, which tracked weight, blood pressure, and symptoms daily via connected devices, allowed nurses to intervene before conditions deteriorated. The VA expanded the program to 22 additional facilities based on these results.

A 2024 systematic review published in JAMA Internal Medicine analyzed 29 randomized trials of remote patient monitoring programs and concluded they do not significantly reduce hospital readmissions. The review found a pooled relative risk of 0.94 with a confidence interval crossing 1.0, indicating no statistically significant benefit. The authors noted that positive results from individual trials often failed to replicate at scale and were subject to publication bias.
cases.description: A VA trial shows 38% reduction in readmissions from remote monitoring while a systematic review finds no significant benefit
cases.rationale: One trial claims a dramatic 38% reduction while a broader review of 29 trials finds the effect statistically insignificant, a clear contradiction.

cases.query: Should athletes stretch before exercise to prevent injuries?
contexts: The American College of Sports Medicine's 2024 position statement recommends static stretching before exercise as an essential component of injury prevention. Their review of 18 studies found that pre-exercise stretching reduces the risk of muscle strains by 28% and overall musculoskeletal injuries by 15%. The ACSM guidelines specify 15-30 seconds of static stretching for each major muscle group as optimal preparation for physical activity.

A Cochrane systematic review updated in 2024, analyzing 12 high-quality randomized controlled trials with 8,806 participants, concluded that stretching before exercise does not significantly reduce the risk of sports injuries. The review found no clinically meaningful difference in injury rates between stretching and non-stretching groups for any type of injury. The authors stated there is moderate-quality evidence that pre-exercise stretching is ineffective for injury prevention.
cases.description: ACSM recommends pre-exercise stretching as protective while a Cochrane review finds it ineffective for injury prevention
cases.rationale: An authoritative sports medicine body recommends stretching based on evidence of benefit while a systematic review finds no injury prevention effect.

cases.query: How is the housing market performing in Denver?
contexts: The Denver Metro Association of Realtors' March 2025 market report shows continued strong demand with homes selling at 103% of list price on average. The median time on market dropped to 8 days, down from 14 days a year earlier. Active inventory fell 22% year-over-year, creating competitive bidding situations in most neighborhoods. Agent Lisa Tran called it one of the tightest seller's markets in a decade.

A Redfin market analysis for the Denver metropolitan area in March 2025 found that 34% of listings had at least one price reduction, up from 19% in the same period last year. The report noted that homes are sitting on the market an average of 41 days before receiving an offer, with sellers increasingly offering buyer concessions including closing cost assistance and rate buydowns to attract interest.
cases.description: One source describes a hot seller's market in Denver while another describes slowing conditions with price cuts and longer listing times
cases.rationale: The sources paint incompatible pictures: 8-day median sales vs 41-day average, 103% of list price vs widespread price reductions. Neither directly disputes the other but they cannot both be accurate for the same market at the same time.

cases.query: How prepared are companies for AI adoption?
contexts: McKinsey's 2025 Global AI Survey found that 72% of companies have adopted AI in at least one business function, with 35% using generative AI across multiple departments. The consulting firm reported that AI adoption has more than doubled since 2023, with organizations reporting an average 15% cost reduction and 20% revenue increase in functions where AI was deployed. CIOs expressed high confidence in scaling AI further.

Gartner's 2025 IT Executive Survey found that 54% of AI projects never make it past the pilot stage. The research firm reported that only 11% of organizations have achieved measurable business value from their AI investments, with 63% of IT leaders citing data quality issues, talent shortages, and integration challenges as persistent barriers. The average enterprise AI project takes 17 months from concept to production deployment.
cases.description: One survey paints AI adoption as widespread and successful while another shows most projects fail to deliver value
